doc.title: Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01

title: Oliver's playing and the 1931 Frederick Brothers tour
summary: Paul says Oliver could still play, then recounts the 1931 bus trip to Wichita, pay cuts, and his return to New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Before you go on, I wanted to ask a little bit about Joe Oliver. How he was playing. Was he as good as before? I mean was he getting worse with his teeth or could he still play real well? What did you think of it?
He could play real well then.

Real well then. And then later I'll come to the part where he began to fail. So after leaving Quag, after that job was up, then it was up to 1930. You see I played around with different bands up until 1931. I was playing with Richard Cheaterman in what you call a taxi dancing school they called up there. Then King Oliver came back with the band and asked me to make a trip with him. That was in 1931. Well John Marrero was to go on the trip but he was in bed with the union. He didn't make the trip. So in 1931 we had a contract with Frederick Brothers and we left New York, I think it was in May, to go to Wichita Kansas. I mean yeah Wichita Kansas they had Frederick Brothers. One of the longest rides I ever had in my life, halfway across the United States in a bus. Three days we were riding. Well we got over there and we were very much disappointed because we were supposed to get fifty dollars a week. But they wouldn't give us, but then one man said he wouldn't pay but forty dollars a week because King Oliver couldn't play the records when he was supposed to play because Dave Nelson, he had gotten in bed with King and he took all his arrangements. So King hit out on the road without any arrangements. And then the man said well we represent you to play these records but the new band he had couldn't play the records. So that cut us down. Well we did pretty good and the depression was on pretty strong then. It was pretty strong. Things got so bad that the man actually couldn't pay forty dollars a week. And then when they said when they cut the band down to fifty dollars a week King Oliver lost half of his good men. They all went back to New York. So he got another bunch of fellas and then when the man wanted to cut it down to thirty dollars a week then they left. So things was pretty bad so I told Simon at that time they had King Oliver had sent to New Orleans and got Simon Marrero. So I told Simon that I think I'm going to go back to New Orleans. That was the end of 1931. I said around Christmas time. I said I'm going back to New Orleans. Simon said yeah you do pretty good back in New Orleans. So I left King Oliver's band but when I left his band then his band was just gone to nothing. Everybody had left just had about five or maybe six or seven piece out of a fifteen piece band left. And they just playing a little job around which he wasn't doing anything. So I came to New Orleans and I got here and one of the saxophone players came down with me Walter Dennis. His name was he came down to New Orleans but things wasn't too good in New Orleans and Walter Dennis went back. I stayed around New Orleans and I worked around with different bands. I played with Mealy, Spain and with Abby Williams, George Williams and many others. It takes a lot of time to call them all. I have it all marked down to Willie Pajos, Melody Boys and so forth.
